core: Working definition, attributed: SQLite's language reference states that a SELECT statement enclosed in parentheses is a subquery; Microsoft Learn adds that a subquery is a query nested inside a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement, or inside another subquery
Inner/outer terminology, attributed: Microsoft Learn calls the nested query the inner query (inner select) and the statement containing it the outer query (outer select)

Why subqueries exist: some questions are answered in steps, and a subquery packs both steps into one statement; original example — find products priced above the average price, built from two steps into one nested statement

The basic shape: an inner SELECT in parentheses feeding an outer SELECT; the inner result is used as a value or a list; SQLite documents that an uncorrelated subquery is evaluated only once and the result reused as necessary
Subqueries with WHERE: the most common placement; the mechanism stated simply — a condition built from another query's result (W3Schools on IN with a subquery; W3Schools and PostgreSQL on EXISTS)

Subqueries versus joins: one-line contrast — a join combines tables side by side, a subquery nests one query inside another; Microsoft Learn states many statements with subqueries can alternatively be formulated as joins; join mechanics owned by the join topic, referenced only
Readability and honest framing: nesting hides logic, so keep subqueries short and shallow; a subquery is a tool, not a goal — when a join reads more clearly, prefer it
supporting: Parentheses are the marker of a subquery: PostgreSQL — subqueries specifying a derived table must be enclosed in parentheses
IN's right-hand side must be a parenthesized subquery returning exactly one column (PostgreSQL 9.24.2 Subquery Expressions)
EXISTS returns true when the subquery returns at least one row (PostgreSQL 9.24.1; W3Schools)
A subquery can be used anywhere an expression is allowed (Microsoft Learn); this lesson keeps to the WHERE placement
outOfScope: JOIN syntax and mechanics (own topic: join; referenced only for the contrast)
Aggregate functions such as AVG (own topic: aggregate-functions; used only as a known tool in the average example, never taught)
Correlated subqueries and subqueries inside INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE

claims.claim: SQLite's language reference defines a subquery as a SELECT statement enclosed in parentheses.
Microsoft Learn defines a subquery as a query that is nested inside a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement, or inside another subquery, and calls the statement containing it the outer query.
W3Schools explains that IN can be used with a subquery in the WHERE clause: the main query returns all records that are present in the result of the subquery.

W3Schools states that the EXISTS operator is used in a WHERE clause to check whether a subquery returns any rows; PostgreSQL says the subquery is evaluated to determine whether it returns any rows, with a true result when at least one row comes back.
Microsoft Learn states that many statements that include subqueries can alternatively be formulated as joins, while other questions can be posed only with subqueries.
PostgreSQL documents that the right-hand side of IN is a parenthesized subquery, which must return exactly one column.
SQLite documents that an uncorrelated subquery is evaluated only once and the result reused as necessary.
PostgreSQL states that subqueries specifying a derived table must be enclosed in parentheses.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources phrase the same concept differently: SQLite defines a subquery as a SELECT statement enclosed in parentheses, Microsoft Learn defines it as a query nested inside another statement, and PostgreSQL describes subqueries as derived-table expressions that must be parenthesized.
positions: SQLite: 'A SELECT statement enclosed in parentheses is a subquery'
Microsoft Learn: 'A subquery is a query that is nested inside a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement, or inside another subquery'
PostgreSQL: subqueries must be enclosed in parentheses
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three describe the same nesting idea. The lesson uses SQLite's phrasing as the working definition, Microsoft Learn's inner-query/outer-query terminology for the parts, and PostgreSQL's note for why the parentheses matter, treating the three phrasings as one agreed concept.
